ON OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

### On the images of the head and tail of the Moon's dragon. Chap. XLV.

<note>A woodcut depicts a serpent coiled into a circle resembling the Greek letter Theta. The creature has the head of a hawk and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, a vertical line is crossed by a shorter horizontal line, marked with small symbolic points at the ends.</note>

They also used to make an image of the head and tail of the Moon's dragon <note>the lunar nodes, where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note>, namely the figure of a serpent between an airy and a fiery circle, with the head of a hawk surrounding them in the likeness of the Greek letter theta. They made it when Jupiter held the midheaven with that head; they affirm that this image contributes much to the success of petitions. By this image, they intended to denote a good and fortunate spirit <term>daemon</term> <gloss>a spiritual entity or guardian</gloss>, and they wished to figure it through the image of a serpent, for the Egyptians and Phoenicians celebrated this as the most divine animal above all others, and praised its divine nature. This is because a sharper and more expansive spirit of fire exists in it above other animals, which is shown by its swift gait without any feet, hands, or other instruments, and because it repeatedly renews its age and becomes young again. They made an image of the tail in a similar way when the Moon was eclipsed in the tail, or badly affected by Saturn or Mars; they made it to induce anxiety and infirmity, and they called it an evil spirit. A certain Hebrew had included such an image in a double golden belt, which Blanche, the daughter of the Duke of Bourbon, gave as a gift to her husband Peter, the first king of Spain of that name, whether knowingly or unknowingly. When he was girded with it, he seemed to himself to be encircled by a serpent, and having subsequently discovered that a magic power had been inserted into the belt, he repudiated his wife for that reason.

### On the images of the mansions of the Moon. Chap. XLVI.

They also used to make images in each of the individual mansions of the Moon. In the first, for the destruction of someone, they made an image in an iron ring of a black man clothed in sackcloth and girded, throwing a small lance with his right hand; they sealed it in black wax and fumigated it with liquid storax and prayed. In the second, against the anger of a prince and for his reconciliation, they sealed in white wax and mastic the image of a crowned king, and fumigated it with wood of aloes. In the third, they made an image in a silver ring whose measure was square and whose figure was a woman well-dressed, sitting on a chair, with her right hand raised above her head; they sealed and fumigated it with musk, camphor, and aromatic nail <note>likely clove or a specific shell-based incense ingredient</note>. They asserted that this bestows prosperity of fortune and every good thing. In the fourth, for vengeance and separation, enmity and malevolence, they sealed in red wax the image of a soldier sitting on a horse, holding a serpent in his right hand, and fumigated it with red myrrh and storax. In the fifth, for the favor of kings and officials and a good reception, they sealed from silver the head of a man, and fumigated it with sandalwood. In the sixth, for placing love between two, they sealed in white wax two images embracing one another, and fumigated it with wood of aloes and amber.
